ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Back up site
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Tim, a full site backup comes in three parts, the database , the moodledata folder and the code itself. you need the first two to remain contemporary, the code, well, that is not so critical. Not that it is not important, but is less important than maintaining the accurate versioning of the other two. You did not mention what version of Moodle you are using, btw , - that could be important. Are you simply trying to backup and restore an entire site? You said: "I went into my Php Admin in the cPanel and downloaded all of the tables in a . sql file and then uploaded them" So where did you download them from, and where did you upload them to? A private home server , your test Moodle, to a a site? Or the other way around? Site to Site? These things are imprtant too. phpMyAdmin , assuming you are using a MySQL database, allows you to backup the tables with no data, the data with no tables or the data and tables. All three can be in a .sql file or a text file. (.sql for restoring easily would be my guess.) One possible problem is if you used cPanel to restore? cPanel is doing some funny things to Moodle recently. You do not need to muck around with the code, unless you want something absolutely specific to your site. Otherwise the only changes you may want to make are such things as new themes, modification of the occasional block, new activity types. The core code though, does not really need much more than a superficial tweak.  For example, if you want to use the line command for a TeX page, you need to remove the word "line" from the list of forbidden words. Some of these are listed in the Beginning Administration FAQ - if you care to look. Thik about these issues and see what it is that you really have done and what you really want to do. Let us know.. someone can help, but only if you are really clear about it.

Any ideas? 2) The file sizes of the backups for the courses being backed up are tiny, even though I have them set to back up all the user files, etc. For example, I just did a manual backup for one of my classes, and it resulted in a 21MB .mbz file. Looking down to the "Automated Bakup" list, the last backup for this class was a 2.1MB .mbz file. That is absolutely impossible, as some of the PDFs of materials I host in the course are almost 10MB. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Automated Course Backup Weirdness [Moodle 2.0.2]
ResponsesInList.Text: 1) I don't know. 2) This is an intentional design decision. Because of the way files are stored in Moodel 2.x, there is no need to include the files in the backup if you are planning to restore them to the same Moodle site. Leaving them out saves huge amounts of disc space and makes the backup procedure much faster.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Automated Course Backup Weirdness [Moodle 2.0.2]
ResponsesInList.Text: So, can you clarfiy this for me.  I actually set my backups to backup to the course and to a folder that is offsite.  It appears that the offsite backups are a good size so does Moodle automatically include the files in an offsite backup but then not include them on the local course backups?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Automated Course Backup Weirdness [Moodle 2.0.2]
ResponsesInList.Text: I don't know exactly how this works. I have just picked up bits of it in passing from other people's conversations. Backups have various purposes, but I think the automated overnightbackups are mainly about being able to recover if something goes disasterously wrong. And in terms of disaster recovery, there are really two main scenarios to worry about: 1. Something goes disasterously wrong with your whole Moodle server. For example a hard drive failure. In this case, you don't want individual course backups, you want a Site_backup that you can restore. 2. A teacher comes to you and says 'Help, I accidentally deleted the quiz I spent all day yesterday creating'. This is where the automated course backups help. You can selectively restore just that one activity from that one backup file. And, for case 2., even if the activity was deleted, the files will still be in the Moodle file pool, so they don't need to be in the backup file. The automatic backup will just have all the data that was in the database for that course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: White screen of death after restore to 1.9.9
ResponsesInList.Text: Ahh sorry, I have just been berating others for exactly that sin..duh!!!! cPanel has in it somewhere a phpMyAdmin and if you open that, it should allow you access to the database you are using for Moodle.There should be a list of accessible databases, so click on Moodle. (If you only have one db then it might just open in it.) The tables are down the left side and a second listing showing some more information about them is on the right. Check that the Type collumn is InnoDB and the Collation collumn reads utf8_general_ci, these are usualy the 5th and 6th collumns btw . Fantastico has been changing the collation to something wierd like latin1_swedish_ci. Scroll to the bottom of that page, and it should tell you that there is 198 tables or so. There should be about 260+ tables for Moodle 2 so if you have more than 200 tables then it is likely that Fantastico has made a mess of it. The chances of a safe rcovery have dropped considerably, unfortunately, if this is the case. If it is just the collation, then it can be changed, but how depends on what restrictions are placed on you as the admin. If you have full permissions then you can go to the Database page then to the SQL tab. In the dialog box enter this code: say database name ="moodle" ALTER DATABASE 'moodle' DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf-8_unicode_ci; Then press Go. That should work, I emphasise should as my SQL is a little rusty but if you want further help, the MySQL help file will do it. Btw, this cannot be done inside the database, apparently it is some kind of security restriction or some such so it has to be done in the database page. I am not sure how to get around that problem, but your host could tell you. The config.php file is a little easier. Open it in a text editor, but not Windows Notepad or WordPad, in something like Notepad++. You need to look for lines that read: $CFG-> wwwroot = ' http://xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx/moodle' ; $CFG-> dirroot = 'Drive:/server/path/to/your/moodle'; $CFG-> dataroot = 'Drive:/server/path/toyour/moodledata'; Differnet servers use different slashes, so do not edit them. Also, the dirroot may read something like $CFG->dirroot   = userpath  +'/to/your/moodle'; but if this is the one then there will be a declaration like this in the config.php file. $CFG->userpath = 'some/thing/here' There are a number of variations here. If these are not right then you need to edit these to show the path and appropriate ip address. Sorry, that is all for now, I gotta get back to work.. cheers..

Perhaps it is 6 of one and half dozen of the other. The main issue is that the first database, of 213 tables is likely to be the one you need to connect to. The second is more likely to be the Moodle 2 db and that is the one that the config.php file would be trying to connect to I would suspect. It is not working because the calls to the database are different in Moodle 2 than they were in v1.9.x, but if you have the database then there is life yet. I was looking at phpMyAdmin yesterday and found it is a lot more flexible than it used to be and can save files that were previously lost. Now you can open the smaller database and back up the data only or the whole database, using the Operations tab.  Go through the output format options carefully and you can reformat it to a utf8_general_ci charset. If you do not want to try that, just backup the data, create a new database and populate it with the backed up data - but be aware that the database you are restoring data to has to have some generated tables so I would suggest do both data only and entire database. In v1.9.9 if you have your moodledata folder then you have all the images and if all you really need are the quizzes, then you may want to try using the Operations tab to backup just the question tables and when you have your new install up, restore them. Good luck...

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle 1.9 Backup & Restore Question
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone, I am a Moodle newbie. One of the first pieces of advise that I received here was to build my system and make sure it works before uploading it to go live. I've been building a Moodle system on my computer with MAMP , and now that it is setup I need to 'backup' the entire system and 'restore' it to the server where it will live and operate. I am getting confusing/conflicting descriptions of what I need to do, so I am hoping that someone here can explain the steps more clearly - or direct me to a resource that does. To be clear, I want to transfer the whole system - users, modules, theme, logos, quizzes and other content. Thank you all in advance for your reply! Jason

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle 1.9 Backup & Restore Question
ResponsesInList.Text: It is confusing because you do not do it from within Moodle itself, it is an external process. We are used to doing this all internally, but all PHP Apps are different. Backing up the site is different than backing up courses, backing up the front page and so on. The language of PHP Apps is somewhat confusing here, but it is an external process and it is actually safer that way. I am sorry, I thought we went through this in an earlier discussion. The backup occurs in three parts one is the database , one is the moodle core and the last is the uploaded files. If you have phpMyAdmin , use that to backup the entire database. You can use the Operations tab, and copy the database, but when you restore it, you have to have phpMyAdmin to restore it, into an existing MySQL server. Alternatively, you can export the tables, restore them to your new Moodle server, then backup the data separately, using the Operations tab, then restore that into your newly restored database as well, into your new server.  Alternatively, again, if you have some other method of backing up and restoring databases, use that. You can then use a zip program to zip up the existing Moodle root into a moodle.zip file - that is the entire /server/htdocs/moodle folder. Then look for the moodledata folder and zip that up as well. Take these three and restore them, one at a time in your new location and make sure that the relationship between your existing moodle folder and the moodledata folder is the same. Once everything is in place, before you open it, go into the config.php file and make sure that your file paths reflect the new locations, i.e. somethng like: $CFG-> wwwroot = ' http://111.111.111.1/moodle19' ; $CFG-> dataroot = 'd:/path/to/your/moodledata/folder/' Everything else should be the same, as long as you do not change the name of the database.  Good luck...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: backup_unique_code missing
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, just a side note. The rationale beyond this problem uses to be that, under some DBs it's needed to adjust the maximum size of the information that can be sent, as far as it uses to default to a really small value. And backup build some in-session structures that are really big. In any case, be noted that, while switching off DB sessions is a solution for backup & restore... the problem will happen in any insert/update going over that size . So it's highly recommended to raise such small default value! Noticeable MySQL defaults to 1MB, so any insert/update of information bigger that that, will cause, for sure, problems, and worst of all, it uses to do it silently, cutting the information without further notice. Luckily it can be adjusted by setting the max_allowed_packet variable in the my.cnf configuration file (I've it set to 50M, for example). Don't forget to restart the My SQL server after that. Finally, since Moodle 1.9.7 (I think), there is one built-in system on restore that detects if something have been broken in session informing you with this message: "Some problem happened with the restore information stored in your session. Please check your PHP memory/DB package size limits. Restore stopped." And stopping the process before causing any further damage. Hope this explains a bit the session thing and the problems in backup and restore. Ciao

ResponsesInList.Title: Enrol instances (enrol table records) not created from 1.9 course backups in 2.1 install
ResponsesInList.Text: My supervisor restored a large number of courses via 1.9 backups into our new 2.1 install. The courses themselves appear to have restored just fine. However, when I try to update them via web services, I run into an error message: "Manual enrolment plugin instance doesn't exist or is disabled for the course (id = {$a->courseid})" I poked around in the code and I discovered that it was because of a missing enrol table records. When a new course is created, enrol records are created for each authorization plugin you have enabled. When these courses were restored, rather than being created, however, these records were not created. I've reported this as a bug here: http://tracker.moodle.org/browse/MDL-28394

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Enrol instances (enrol table records) not created from 1.9 course backups in 2.1 install
ResponsesInList.Text: I am not sure it is a bug, actually. The backup process restores courses but not user files or records. It is safe to assume that this also means that all records relating to students and enrollments have not been restored. I would suggest that if you are desparate to restore students to courses, then you stay with v 1.9.x until the end of your scholastic year. A general comment: Talking to a lot of people from the northern hemisphere, they are discussing making the changeover to Moodle 2.3 (probably) in June of 2012. As for those in the southern hemisphere, they are discussing the likelihood of a December 2011-January 2012 change to v2.2. For most countries these periods represent the major break and/or end of scholastic year so it is easier to take and close records and just roll out new courses, or backed up courses, new enrollments, new students etc. There are a number of reasons given for this, but for many the difficulty in the backup and restore process has been a factor in that decision. It can be anticipated that this is a temporary situation and will be fully resolved in v2.2 or if it is not ready then, November-December 2011, then for v2.3, June 2012.  That is the release schedule, and from what MD said at this week's MoodleMootAu that will not change. What might change is the features in those releases, that is if a new or revamped feature is ready, it will be released in the major version track, ie 2.2 or 2.3 or 2.4, not in the minor fixes of 2.2.1 or 2.3.3 and so on. The implication is that every 5 years there will be a major revision of Moodle so we go through this again in 4.5 years..

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Enrol instances (enrol table records) not created from 1.9 course backups in 2.1 install
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the reply, Colin. Enrolment instances are created for each type of enrolment that is permitted.  For example, when creating a new course, as our LMS is currently configured, the following three types of enrolment records are created per course: manual guest self To rectify the situation, I have written a script that for all courses, and for all three of those types of enrolments, will create the missing records, if any.  This worked, and solved me problem.  After that, the users, once again, can be enrolled into courses. So, I do think it is a bug, because these enrol records are not directly related to student/teacher enrolments, but rather, they are records informing the system as to what kind of enrolments are permitted per course.

ResponsesInList.Title: Simple backup scripts for Moodle site
ResponsesInList.Text: Apologies if this topic has been covered before I couldn't find anything on the forum exactly the same. Here are a couple of simple backup scripts which will do a complete weekly backup in tar.gz format and incremental daily backup. They also delete old weekly backups (one month) and daily (older than 7 days). The scripts are for linux servers. Replace MY SQL READUSER and MYSQLPASSWORD with your own database user with read access to the moodle database. You should have a backup path available and substitute this for the backup path in the script. Place the daily script in /etc/cron.daily and the weekly in /etc/cron.weekly you will also need to make the scripts executable: # chmod +x daily.sh # chmod +x weekly.sh I have the following backup targets which are samba shares on a NAS: /moodlebackups/daily /moodlebackups/weekly You can easily extend this to backup multiple moodle installations. Comments and Improvements would be most welcome. Scripts included as text below: #!/bin/sh # #Moodles backup script - INCREMENTAL DAILY #created : 14th July 2008 #author : s baxter #moodlebackups is a samba share on backup server # #removes sql files older than a week at the end # Today="`date +%d_%m_%y`"; #moodle - DAILY #!/bin/sh # #Moodles backup script - COMPLETE WEEKLY #created : 14th July 2008 #author : s baxter ##moodlebackups is a samba share on backup server # #removes files older than a month at the end # Today="`date +%d_%m_%y`"; #moodle - WEEKLY sudo mysqldump -uMYSQLREADUSER -pMYSQLPASSWORD moodle > /tmp/moodle_$Today.sql sudo tar -zcpf /tmp/moodle_$Today.tar.gz /var/moodledata /var/www/moodle /tmp/moodle_$Today.sql sudo cp /tmp/moodle_$Today.tar.gz /moodlebackups/weekly/ sudo rm /tmp/moodle_$Today.tar.gz sudo rm /tmp/moodle_$Today.sql sudo find /moodlebackups/weekly -name "*.tar.gz" -mtime +30 -exec rm {} \;

ResponsesInList.Title: Newbie Question about Backup & Restore
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello everyone, While I have spent a couple years using Moodle as a course developer and facilitator, my new position has me wading into the deep waters of Moodle aministration and creating a site from scratch. The place that will eventually host the Moodle system is not yet available, so I was wondering - can I develop the courses and enter user info on my computer (with MAMP ), backup everything, and then restore it on the server where it will finally live? Thank you all in advance for your replies and suggestions! Peace, Jason

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Newbie Question about Backup & Restore
ResponsesInList.Text: Unless you have posted this elsewhere, then, sure you can do that, in fact, I would urge you to do it. For several reasons. Administering a Moodle is, in large part, making sure nothing happens that can go wrong. This means that you have to test things out first. We know that unless Teachers do something absolutely brilliant, they will not usually be in the position of doing anything that can seriously damage the Moodle. Same with Course Creators. Administrators are different - so make sure any Admins are well versed in not doing things that will break the Moodle. This also means that you should have two Moodles, so that you can test stuff before it goes on the production site. You want to add a backup of a course from an unknown source, into your test Moodle first. This allows you to see if there are additional Roles, or Admins assigned that you do not want and so on. It is easier to know what you have to clean up before you put it into your production Moodle. Want to try a new block or filter? Use the test site. When you update the production site, update your test site first, make sure the update works. If something goes wrong, and you do not have time to wade through the problem to fix it, but you know it is in a specific area of your Moodle, and you test site does not show a problem, then just use the code from the test site to replace the flawed code on the production site. You are using a MAMP, but your production site is a LAMP did you say? Can you set up a virtual server on your Mac? These are the sorts of issues that will drive you crazy, but well worth the effort. Of course, the other benefit is that you can pre-prepare stuff for when you are ready to go live. Good luck...

ResponsesInList.Title: Suggestion for student records back-ups
ResponsesInList.Text: This subject has been a topic of discussion since 2003 and, as far as I can tell, it has never really been adequately addressed in any of the builds:  Most schools of any type are required to maintain student records for several years (in our case it is 4 years).  The records for online courses must include all student information, activity and the results of any assignments, quizzes or tests.  Moodlers have recommended the back-up of the entire course with user data and activity logs for future restore, if necessary.  This, however, presents a problem, since some students take more than one course and conflicts are created when restoring a course with user data if the user is already on the system for another course. Perhaps you could come up with a system by which we could separately store and retrieve student activity logs only.  Test results, assignments, student information and other information can be printed out and saved separately in hard copy or in a separate database .  It is the activity logs that take up a lot of space, yet we still have to keep them for 4 years in case we are audited, to show that the student completed all the requirements and spent the minimum amount of time in the course. Thanks for listening.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: how to best make Moodle setup for the fastest disaster recovery. And if it’s possible to have a ‘spare’ server waiting.
ResponsesInList.Text: Nicole - To a certain degree this is a bit more complicated than it may initially seem. There are three major pieces to be backed up. First is having a backup webserver where you could have some type of load balancing. So if you have one webserver go down the load would get shifted over to the other(s). The next piece is the database server and depending on the database you are using there are various ways to setup some type of mirroring and rollover. The final piece is the files in moodledata which are stored on a file system. Could you provide a little more information about your instalation and perhaps some others can help fill in the details particular for your setup. Peace - Anthony

ResponsesInList.Text: Not quite what you want but here is a "poor man's" version of what you want. Set up server (old notebook?) on the internet with a Moodle site. Mine is running Windows and I am using a folder c:\moodle to hold the data on the source and target servers. Every once in a while ( nightly ? hourly?) run this script.  Replace "site" with the name of your site (and your database name) and "ppp" with your MySql root password. del site.bck1 rename site.bck site.bck1 "c:\program files\my sql \mysql server 5.1\bin\mysqldump" -u root -ppp site > c:\moodle\site.bck del moodledata1.zip rename moodledata.zip moodledata1.zip pkzip c:\moodle\moodledata -rP \inetpub\ wwwroot \site\moodledata\*.* xcopy *.* e:\*.* /d /y Here e: is a SD card in the computer. At any point, these files can be copied (over the network or from the SD card) and restored onto another server with this script: "c:\program files\mysql\mysql server 5.1\bin\mysql" -u root -ppp site < c:\moodle\site.bck c: cd \ pkunzip -o \moodle\moodledata (Note: Some pkzip files require pkunzip -d ....)

The regular cron needs to keep running as well of course because it also does all the other little jobs like triggering the mailer.

Moodle is based in the idea of "write once - read anywhere" Web technologies, obviously, be we still need to remind ourselves of that. The technologies themselves are not that great yet, the hardware and software limitations are constraining development, which is obvious here. PHP cannot handle that size file (yet) so how do you deal with it? Am I right in thinking that until this is resolved then you are unable to do a site backup at all? The only thing I can suggest is that the course is broken down into several smaller courses, perhaps one lesson per course. Using a metacourse structure will resolve login issues and if it means the the author is inconvenienced a little, well tough. If average course is around the 500mb range, then that is the price that has to be paid to continue the good order of the site and the fulfilment of the responsibilities of the Administrator, (you?). <soapbox id="interfering sage busybody"> As an aside, I know I have no idea of the circumstances as to how this happened in the first place, but I am somewhat appalled that any Course Creator or Editing-Teacher would allow a course to get so large. To me this suggests poor course design and structure, a definite lack of forethought, or worse, understanding, about the impact of the materials used in the course.  I know videos can get large, easily, and in many courses, videos are an absolute godsend. Camtasia, CamStudio or even Wink will produce small tight videos for any one thing. I suspect that these videos are showing high quality, multistep processes or something similar. Can these be broken down into atomic components? That is what I am telling all the teachers who are asking about making their own videos for Moodle. Each video is, I am suggesting, a self-contained specific purpose video that should not last any more than about 5 minutes (2-3 minutes is, I suspect, about best). I would suggest that hand made movies can be broken into individual scenes that last little more than 5 minutes. I would contend that, with some effort, even Hollywood blockbusters can be broken down into individual clips with very few scenes that last more than that. NatGeo specials, well that would be a challenge.. </soapbox>

ResponsesInList.Text: If backups are handled by your IT staff, then may be you should backup your site and forget backing up individual courses through Moodle. The latter seems better for archiving but with restore restrictions which invariably come with newer Moodle versions, that is of limited utility in reality. When backing up the site as the site, IT people can dump the database into sql or xml file and tar or whatever the moodledata and moodle program directories, and backup the three. This gives full restore now and makes it possible to recreate the site to access content in the future, so it can be used for both running and archival backups. The important aspect here is that working on the back-end, the IT people are not subject to the memory limits, script timeouts, etc that Moodle scripts are.

We didn't see this problem before 2.02 (Build 20110427), so I'm guessing that it's new: we can't reproduce it on the Moodle Demo site where an earlier version is running. However, there is no permission (as far as I'm aware) to deny the deleting of a course as part of the restore process. We really don't have a need for full deletes prior to restore, other than at a moodle admin level. And as the full delete has the ability to wipe out grades in the gradebook, it was quite a risk, given that all our assessment is now online, in the gradebook! So, assuming you've also denied 'course creation' capabilities, you could wrap lines 217 and 228 (or thereabouts) of backup/restore_form.html in if statements like: if ($cancreatecourses) { ...etc... } Doing this limits the options in the drop down box to only 2 - 'Current course, adding data to it' and 'Existing course, adding data to it'. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No after_restore() for course formats in Moodle 2?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Urs, thanks for pinging! Yes, all restore steps (modules, blocks), plugins (themes, course formats, qtypes...) and subplugins (assignment types, workshop evaluations, data fields...) have support, on restore, for hooking code in the "after_execute" methods. So, once one XML file has been completely parsed, all the available "after_execute" methods are invoked, first the ones present in plugins and subplugins and, finally the one in the restore_step itself (that you have not access to modify, it is core). So I guess that you will need (for course formats, having 3 "hooks" defined) one/some methods like: after_execute_course() after_execute_section() after_execute_module() in your course format restore implementation, and all them will be executed, if available, at the end of the process of the XML file, when everything is already loaded in DB, ready for your extra handling. The "course" one will be executed (once) after loading the course.xml information, the "section" (multiple) after loading each section.xml and the "module" (multiple) after loading each module.xml. For reference, I think that, right now, we are using those after_execute_xxx() methods only in some qtype plugins, look for "after_execute_question" for them. Also, you can take a look to "launch_after_execute_methods" functions, where the hook mechanism is somehow explained, just in case you are interested. And that's all I can say, note "after_execute" methods are different from "after_restore" ones because the formers are executed after one XML (restore step) has been processed, so you only can handle information processed by that XML. In the other side, the laters are executed at the end of the whole restore process (but plugins & subplugins have not access to them at all, only modules - complete restore_step citizens - have). At least until now. And that's all, hope it helps...ciao

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Some advice for a complete backup novice please
ResponsesInList.Text: Charlotte hi! If you have backup copies of separate courses, this is all you need. Each backup contains the entire content of the course. You need to do the following: - install a fresh copy of Moodle (compatible with your backups - either 1.9 or 2.0); - upload and restore your course backups. If you are not sure, you can create a local installation of Moodle (on WAMP /XAMPP) and try restoring ONE course. If it works out you can be sure it will work as well on the production server . Moreover: you can email one backup (preferably the smallest) to someone who has a compatible working installation, requestion to restore it. If it restores completely (including the documents - Word, PPT, Excel files, videos, images etc.) you can go ahead and recreate the site almost without losses. You may lose your front page settings, but that will be all, I think. Just my $.02. Best - Lev

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What folders/files back up what? I'm trying to reduce what I need to backup
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Billy I can advise what we do in terms of backup and my understanding of what you need to do but please welcome other's comments too! Users and grades are stored in the database and user files (eg assignment submissions) are stored in the moodledata folder (1.9x) so you should backup the database and the moodledata folder.  There is one numbered folder for each course which has all documents including student's attachments and assignment uploads.  There are also other folders including user and group pictures at this level which you could backup too. 1) We backup the moodle database and the moodledata folder several times a day - this is done as part of normal database and file backup proceedures at our University. 2) We make use of the automated course backups which are part of Moodle core.  We have these backups run daily. They are saved to a folder inside the moodledata folder and we have it configured to keep 1 copy.  At the end of each semester we copy these Moodle backup files to disc for archive purposes.  Tou can configure what you'd like to save in these backup files via the settings page (eg users, user data (eg assignment submission docs, logs, etc). 3) We duplicate our entire Moodle site on a weekly basis to our testing site - this might sound a little overboard and is essentially done for testing purposes.  I have found this is a great backup for me as the Administrator as I've needed to refer to this site several times for teachers who have deleted things before! The Moodle code doesn't change so I would only back this up every now and then and definately before you complete an upgrade.  We use git to control our code.  In terms of upgrades we also backup the database before performing one so we can revert if needed. So basically, I recommend backing up the database & the moodledata folder on a regular basis I hope this helps! Cheers Teresa

ResponsesInList.Title: Ang: Backing up questions only
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Nancy You can share questions between courses (which is what I assume will solve your problem) if you store them in a context that can be reached from those courses. So if your questions is located in a categori in a course, you can move them to a category at a higher level, eg. site level. Read more in Moodle Docx about Question categories Be aware that participants (normally teachers) have to have the appropiate permissions. See How to let teachers share questions between courses

ResponsesInList.Text: Use the quetsion bank import/export for this, using Moodle XML format.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Restore ISSUE in Moodle 1.9.11
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, my immediate response is to go back to the original courses and back them up and try restoring them again, if they are available. If not then a different strategy needs be applied. Get away from your production site, this is done in your test Moodle. (If you have no test Moodle then find the same version as your production site and install it on your local machine - that becomes your test Moodle. When you update your production site, update your test Moodle, keep them in tandem, btw , the OS for this does not really matter it is Moodle being tested, not the environment. If you no longer have the same version, and you cannot get it, download and use the latest 1.9.xx, bare bone restores will work - but they have to be absolutely bare boned - course files and nothing else - no users, no user files, no site files.) Whatever you decide, and someone else may have a better alternative here, it is going to cost a bit of time to rebuild the courses using the backup, but not as much if you were to rebuild them from new. 1) Unzip the backup zip into an empty folder. You should then have access to all the files in the zip, if you do not, the zip is probably corrupt and you may have another set of problems. If you do, check the Moodle. xml file - make sure it has everything in it that is supposed to be there. 2) Check the header information against a backup of your own. See if the data is right or not. Try to restore into your test Moodle and if that does not work, surprise, then unzip it into your test Moodle, reconstruct the course.  If it does work, then rezip it and use the new backup to restore to the production site. 3) Even if the backup is corrupt, or if other bits are missing, here is something I did once and maybe fluked it - it worked but I have no idea why or how and as it did, I looked like a genius, but really, I was playing and got it to work - although it was only a very small course, about 20 images and some five or six topics, no quizzes and one forum I think and about four activities . Small indeed. I backed up a course that I created specifically to match this broken backup. I used the same names and types for each element and then backed up the created course in the Moodle the course was going into. I then copied over the  course files, leaving the site and  moddata files and put everything between the <DESCRIPTION> and </DESCRIPTION> tags. The only thing I was really changing in the new Moodle.xml file was the information of the courses. If I remember right, I also tried to fix the paths to the course files in the text editor but I am not sure if it worked. I cannot remember manually going through and replacing the images, but who knows.  This was a bit of work and I had time to do it then, I doubt I would now. If your courses are not big, then perhaps this may work for you, if you know how the courses are constructed or if you can properly read the original xml file.

Therefore in some situations  the links will be broken, and they will look like this https://somemoodleurl/course/$@FORUMVIEWBYID*750359@$, and in other cases Moodle will successfully decode them, and link properly to the new forum IDs. This bug had been reported before, and I can confirm that I can replicate it on Moodle 1.9.8+ (Build: 20100407) Plus, I've found this MDL-19295 and MDL-27018 I would advise to try different backup settings, e.g. I broke mine when I have included only parts of my course in the backup. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MOODLE offline CD-ROM course  for use on ships in the Caribbean sea?
ResponsesInList.Text: Tomas, Here's where you can download my latest version I call it Portable Moodle. It's going to be way easier to use than Micro web and there's basically nothing to do. It's fully documented. Download link below: username 'seeker' password 'manna' http://svn.serveall.net/releasecatalog/public/lt/tools/Portable%20Moodle/Latest%20Install/EN/ Now after you download it and run the executable it will install the full version (500mb) which includes all the development tools I used to create it (all open source & Freeware). By default it installs in c:\pm1.20en. It will run straight away from your hard drive. If you want to burn a CD ROM with it there are two simple ways: 1. Just go to c:\pm1.20en\System\mode_cd.bat (hit enter to pass questions) this prepares it for CD, then burn your CD you can use the portable burner I included in c:\pm1.20en\System\Extra\DeepBurner Portable. 2. Run the install from the PStart menu which will install the mini version which is 135mb but unfortunately it will attempt to install it to c:\pm1.20en by default just change the path to something like .._mini or something different. Then repeat procedure with mode_cd.bat in number 1. Then burn your CD. If you use method number 1 you will have a full CD with all dev tools which will be about 500 mb. Method 2 will only be 135 mb all dev tools left out. If you get lost click on help on PStart menu which has all the help you ever wanted. One note: When you start adding content to moodle you want to be in read/write mode run \System\mode_us.bat which puts you in read/write mode which is indicated on the PStart menu by the icon that looks like a hdd. Then after you've got your content set the way you want it you then execute the \System\mode_cd.bat then burn your CD. Again if you need more detail launch the help files on the PStart menu. Let me know what you think or if you have any problems. John

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: BACKUP Issues
ResponsesInList.Text: OK, stop doing what you are doing. You are probably adding to the problem. Understand that you have not really provided a lot of information here so the responses here are either  a shotgun approach or a guess, which may or may not be of any value to you. As a general observation, when you have any kind of issue, the first thing you can do is to go to Administration > Server > Debugging and turn on Debug messages to "ALL:..." Do whatever is causing the issue and then check the logs. Sometimes this means you can track the problem down and resolve it quickly, or it will point to something that needs further investigation. The information from the logs can then be given here which can help resolve issues more rapidly. Don't forget to turn the Debug Messages off afterward, btw . Now, my guess. Whenever I have had a restore issue it often meant I have a Role, quite often the Admin User Role, that is different and Moodle rejected the restore because it cannot reconcile these two roles. In your backup, go to the zip file and unzip it, open the Moodle. xml file and delete the Admin User Role, the details of it anyway. (Use a UTF-8 compatible text editor, like TextPad or NotePad++ or Crimson Editor anything, but not Windows Notepad.) Save the file, rezip the backup and try a restore. This can also apply to other Roles as well, but usually the Admin User Role is the one that creates the drama. Another issue can be there is a block used in the course and included as a site file in the backup that is not present in the restore Moodle. You may want to find the block, using the same method as above, and delete references to it from the backup. This does not always work, as you can delete something you should not have - be aware of that, and be careful if you do it. Suggestion, run two types of backups, one that is a class changeover, or end of year or semester or course backup that includes ALL user files. Store that backup somewhere off your Moodle and keep it secure. Reset the course then create a second backup without User Data, but when creating the backup, do other things as well. I do NOT include User Data, Users, User Files, Site Files, Logs, Grade Histories, and NO backup Role Assignments. I try and make it as small as possible. It may mean losing some Exercise and Workshop activities , but we do not use a lot of these we use more Lessons anyway. This I store off the Moodle in a separate location and try to keep it safe, and I only keep one of these. This is my first port of call when having a problem in a course. It may mean losing some User data sometimes, if there is no current backup but better that than my courses. It also means courses can be operational again quickly. The other thing is backing up. If a single course is not backing up, then there is often a corrupt file or block somewhere that is causing the issue. If it is restricted to one course then it may even be a course file, go into the course, delete from it any unusual blocks. Look at the files area and see if there is anything unusual in there. If there is, delete it and try again. The shotgun is using your test Moodle. FTP to your Moodle Root and look at the folder structure. You should be able to find the Backup folder, then delete it. From your test Moodle, copy the Backup folder directly to your site using FTP.  This works for a couple of reasons, the connectionless nature fo the Internet, and second, there is not a lot of files in Modle that are installed, these are scripted pages, not executables, so you can replace entire folders or single pages and still have Moodle running properly. If you have no test Moodle then I suggest you create one, the same version, from the same download as your site Moodle. Test things here first, use a smal number of courses to do things with, and do not be afraid of wrecking it. A small Moodle used to test stuff in before you do anything to your site is going to show you problems before you import them to your production site. I usually place this test Moodle on my local machine, environment does not matter much, usually, but sometimes it does. Get a problem on your production site and you can test responses here too. Good luck.

Of course.. sorry, the Admin User is a Role specifically created for a purpose, not by me, by someone else, I came in later, should have remembered.. duh.. my error.. that is why it works for me, appears in my courses but is not a default role. This is the same reason it causes problems... The hints are there, all we have to do is analyse them... You have a problem with a block in a course, turn the block off then it backs up. The block that you turned off, is that a standard block or a third party block? Can you delete it and then replace it with a fresh, newly unzipped, block? How much is it used in other courses? Are you gettign any unusual error messages? Did you turn on Debugging to look if there was any unusual error messages? Some backup problems can occur when something has been updated and something else has not. This can mean third party blocks not properly maintained, and those that are are not always updated if you update your Moodle, can cause issues - and not just in backups. Is this possible in this case?  Has anything else changed? What I have done in the past is to replace sections of a Moodle without updating the whole thing, which can be a risky strategy if you are not using the same version. As it is PHP scripting, you can progressively update or refresh is a better word here, by deleting the existing pages and replacing them with freshly unzipped pages from the same version downloaded file  if you still have it, or download a more recent release and update it manually, one folder at a time (higher risk because of a coding change but it can be beneficial too in updating a Moodle). Backups acting odd, replace the folder, a block problem replace the blocks, all of them, filters, the same. Icons can also cause problems in some things, but not one in backups AFAIK , but they too can be easily replaced. At this point, time is becoming an issue so start stripping stuff, like site files, out of backups. Try different combinations on the courses that are not backing up properly. ResponsesInList.Text: Olá, Venho dar minha contribuição neste portal, espero que seja útil aos administradores. Consiste num script de backups do sistema moodle em geral, para ser implementado no servidor onde está hospedado o sistema. Funciona para qualquer versão do moodle utilizando sistema de banco de dados mysql . []'s @zapdf 1) Criação do arquivo .sh que irá conter as linhas de comando: Em uma pasta específica de administração do sistema crie um diretório dos backups: mkdir /home/backups touch /home/backups/script-backup.sh 2) Editando o arquivo do script. Utilizando seu editor preferido crie um arquivo com as seguintes linhas (neste caso utilizou-se o vi ): vi /home/backups/script-backup.sh #função da data DATE=`date +%Y_%m_%d` # Agendando horário para execução do script. varia da sua política de backups, no caso do exemplo toda sexta feira às 3 da manhã: 0 3 * * fri root /bin/sh /home/backups/script-backup.sh Pronto! Seu script de backups do seu sistma moodle foi implementado. Agora faça suas cópias de segurança e faça as devidas manutenções no servidor. Em breve irei postar como é feita a restauração.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: from 2.0 to 1.9
ResponsesInList.Text: Right now, I understand there is no script to make backups backwards compatible. However, I know that these issues have been discussed and I understand that workarounds are possible, but as the complexities are fairly substantial, I do not know what progress has been made, if any. I understand that v2.1 is supposed to contain a 1.9.x to 2.1 conversion process, but I do not know about the reversal. It is probably not helpful to suggest that previous backups are still compatible, so if you have any courses that have an existing backup, you should be able to restore them without issue. If you do not have such backups, then perhaps you may need to review your backup policies and procedures. I would seriously suggest that you consider a backup at the end of each course, which includes student's submitted work and results. I do not think it matters that you have 20 or thirty copies of the same course, each with different students in it. The only issue is storage, which could be another medium, a DVD, or remote drive created specifically for storing your course and student materials backups, or even both. Whatever you do, it needs be secure and safe and accessible. Sorry if this seems patronizing, but I know large organizations where such issues are not considered, or if they are, they are not considered important, or if they are considered important, they are too important to have some low-ranked worker actually do the work and make sure backups exist. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Another backup problem
ResponsesInList.Text:
I've also had the same backup problems related to unicode in MySQL. Our site uses Japanese in unicode (1.5.2+). Mitsuhiro Yoshida was instrumental in helping me identify the problem and how to solve it. I fixed it using mysqlcheck to check it: $ mysqlcheck -p <password> -u <username> database_name then repair: $ mysqlcheck -r -p <password> -u <username> database_name then optimize: $ mysqlcheck -o -p <password> -u <username> database_name Surprisingly, when I ran the first check, no problems were reported (all tables check out OK).  Nonetheless, I did the repair and optimize anyway, and it
solved my problems. Finally I set up a daily cron to run mysqlcheck to analyze and optimize the database . mysqlcheck -ao -p <password> -u <username> database_name This will probably be unncessary with version 1.6, but for the time being, it's very helpful.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: copy a course
ResponsesInList.Text: Are you copying the course to a new Moodle or replicating on an existing Moodle? Do you want a new course or a direct copy of one? These questions are important as to how you copy then paste the course. If it is a new course on a new Moodle then your best option would be to backup the previous course and include User files, then restore it to your new Moodle and everything should be intact. If you are replicating on an existing Moodle then you perform the same all files included backup, but then when you restore, give it another name, restore it as a new course. If you want a new course, then you can create your new blank course, then import the files of the previous course, but, from meory, this does not always bring over User Files, I think you have to specify User Files as well. Note, in each case, include the User files. If you want a direct copy of the course and all its files then whenever you try to copy and paste, it is probably going to cause problems with replication in the database and moodledata folder, so this is not a preferred option. Any of these options should work as you need.

ResponsesInList.Title: Migrate Moodle 1.9.7 database to Moodle 2.0 MSQL database
ResponsesInList.Text: I have two Moodle servers up and running. Both Windows 2003 servers, the production server is running Moodle 1.9.7 and other server is running Moodle 2.0.Both are slick out-of-the-box setups, nothing really special or custom.  1.9.7 is running off of Apache and 2.0 is using IIS 6.0 and both using MySQL . The versions of MY SQL are what came pre-packaged with the 1.97 and 2.0 downloaded packages.  I want to take the data from the 1.9.7 MSQL and import it into the 2.0 Moodle MSQL database . Also not to mention I also need to move the Moodledata contents and contents of the Moodle folders.  I have reade several forums and just gets confusing the more I read them. I'm primarily a Microsoft admin, not an SQL admin or PHP expert. Getting Moodle to run on IIS in two days was a combination of luck and skill. So...does anyone have a fairly straight forward and simple, comparded to less simple, way to copy the database and all relevant data over from 1.9.7 to 2.0 Moodle? Thanks in advance. David Sierra Vista, AZ

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Migrate Moodle 1.9.7 database to Moodle 2.0 MSQL database
ResponsesInList.Text: The easiest way to do this is: 1. Upgrade a your Moodle 1.9.7 site to Moodle 2.0. 2. Back up all the courses in the upgraded site using the Moodle course backup feature. 3. Restore those backups into the Moodle 2.0 site. As a step 0. it would be a very good idea to make a copy of your Moodle 1.9 site before you start, and perhaps upgrade the clone, not the original site. It should be possible to just backup the courses in the 1.9 site and restore those backups into Moodle 2.0, but restoring 1.9 backups into 2.0 is the most embarrassing missing feature in 2.0 at the moment.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Migrate Moodle 1.9.7 database to Moodle 2.0 MSQL database

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cannot restore 1.x backup to 2.0
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Bob We have upgraded two of our sites recently to Moodle 2.0 from 1.9.10 ( www.moodlemoot.co.nz and www.moodlebites.com ).  This has provided an 'interesting' learning curve(!) - which is very different to starting a fresh Moodle 2.0 site (which we also have, and works quite well). At the moment we have to employ different backup strategies due to the Moodle 2.0 backup problems.  Not ideal.  Of course you need to re-develop a Theme if you have one for 1.9 that is customised. Some small annoying changes - e.g. embedded YouTube video behaviour seems to have changed, images used in topic/week headings work differently, hidden resources in the site main menu have altered behaviour.  Navigation bar - most of our designers are hiding it as it gets in the way, lol.  Oh, and Cloze questions had problems on the upgrade (which is not the first time we've seen this). One of our biggest problems was the change in behaviour within the Lesson . Any 'default' blank jumps now need to specify Next page or something - which means we have to manually edit every Lesson again.  There's a dicussion thread elsewhere on the site about this, and Lesson changes in general. Like I said, it's been a learning curve over the past two months for our designers and facilitators, but I think we understand most of the changes now. Ultimately, if you have a fairly basic course, resources, forums, quizzes, etc. you should be fine upgrading to 2.1.  You won't get 'junk', but you might have to quickly run-through and check everything and make some adjustments.  Even so, I would recommend taking a copy of your site and upgrading that to test exactly what changes, and if you are happy with the tweaking you would then have to do. Hope this helps? Stu.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backing up site to backup_sche_destination
ResponsesInList.Text: Are you running a Windows or a Unix operating system? On Windows you use a normal windows path like: E:\Backups or C:\portal\mybackups If you can, there are certain advantages to using a separate hard drive for your backups. Example, you run Moodle on C: but you save the backups to a separate hard drive on E:. If the main drive on C: fails then your backups are still accessible on the E: drive, thus making your site recovery much easier.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backing up site to backup_sche_destination
ResponsesInList.Text: Ros, You might be exposing your course site to a security vulnerability in what you are proposing to do.  It sounds like you may be putting the backup files in a directory which is directly accessible to a browser.  If so, unencrypted private user or course data could be accessible to unauthorized users.  It's possible to minimize the risks through thoughtful use of directory restrictions in .htaccess files or server configuration files, but you need to think through this carefully. Luis's suggestion to back things up to a physically different hard disk (if one is available) has the double benefit of providing a safer backup in case of disk failure and also isolates the files from direct viewing by others.  If you only have one disk, you could still direct the output to a directory where you could have easy access to the files using secure ftp or secure copy, but without compromising data security.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backing up site to backup_sche_destination
ResponsesInList.Text: If you don't specify a path for the backups in the backup_sche_destination field in Site Administration/Courses/Backups then Moodle will put the backups (.zip files) in the backupdata folder ( Home/Course Name/Files/backupdata ) in each of your courses. If a backup_sche_destination is specified then all the backups will be stored in that folder. If you don't see your backups look at the Last Execution Log under Site Administration/Reports/Backups to see the status of the backups and if they completed successfully. If you click on each of the course names you'll see all the details of the backups for each of the courses.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backing up site to backup_sche_destination
ResponsesInList.Text: I would suggest storing the backups on a separate hard drive and in a folder that's not accessible via the web. This way if your main hard drive fails then you won't lose your backups. A backup folder that's not accesible via the web makes it much harder for a hacker to get to the backups. You haven't specified your OS, but on Windows you specify a drive in the normal Windows format, e.g.: F:\Backups\Moodle. Once a backup_sche_destination path has been specified all your automated backups will be stored in this folder. Manual course backups will still be saved in the individual course folders.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle 2.0.1 how to restore backup courses from the server or web
ResponsesInList.Text: Hans, please understand that Moodle 2.0.x is a complete rewrite, not an upgrade. In doing so, the underpinning structure of Moodle is completely different. I think this was always touted as being the single biggest issue facing the step from 1.9 to 2. For the moment, I would recommend that you tell your admin, creator and teacher staff that moodle 2.0 is available as a test environment. It is hugely different and will need a bit of lead time to get used to. Encourage them to start new courses in Moodle 2.0.x as a test site but keep the Moodle 1.9.x going as a production site for your Users. (This gives everyone time and I would not be surprised if the backup conversion is a separate or even a completely different program.) Just go to Server > Session Handling  and add a different cookie prefix for each Moodle, this allows them to run concurrently on one computer otherwise they get logged out of one Moodle as they log into another, even using different IDs.

ResponsesInList.Title: Can there be a straight-forward conversion script between Backup 1.9 and Backup 2.0
ResponsesInList.Text: The main thing keeping me from testing and then using in my class Moodle 2.0 is the lack of ability for 2.0 to read 1.9 backup files as well as the ability for 2.0 to save its backup in 1.9 format.  The docs say that 1.9 to 2.0 will be a feature in a future version. It would seem like one solution would be to have a script that could read in a 1.9 backup file and output it in 2.0 format and vice-versa.  Not every feature would need to be supported, just those that come from a plain-vanilla 1.9 course with no custom extensions. I can't see any documentation on the backup file format but I want to put out the question (before I try to reverse engineer and make a hack that does this): is there a reason that such a script would not be feasible? --Gary

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can there be a straight-forward conversion script between Backup 1.9 and Backup 2.0
ResponsesInList.Text: Here are my notes about the format of both the 1.9 and 2.0 backup files: 1.9 backups end in .zip.  This file can be unzipped to reveal the structure. Files associated with the backup are located in folders and sub folders including site_files, course_files, moddata (for activities ) and user_files. All data of populating the database for the course is on the top level and is named moodle. xml .  This contains user data, activity descriptions, student and other participants submissions, grades, course details, section details, and role information. For 2.0 2.0 backups have a file ending of .mbz.  However, you can change the ending to .zip to open it. Database information is now divided into a good number of separate xml files; some of these are in folders. Course and user files, etc. are renamed to a hash code name with no extension.  However, you can use the files.xml file on the top level to rename them to their original filename and extension and these can be opened.  All such files are kept in the file directory in subdirectors that are named with the first two characters of the hash code. There is an activity directory with folders for individual activities.  Each of these contain serveral xml files depending on the type of activity. There is a course directory with several xml files and a blocks directory with more folders that have xml files describing the content of the blocks. There is a sections directory with one folder for each section (like week or topic). There are several top level xml files for things like gradebook, group, questions, scales, roles, users, outcomes, and users. The individual xml files seem to individually have very similar fields to the consolidated moodle.xml file of 1.9, but I have not dug into this in depth. So, making a 1.9 to 2.0 conversion script would involve parsing the moodle.xml file and creating a good number of individual xml files and a directory structure.  One would also have to generate a hash code and rename the files and make a files.xml to point individual files to their course locations. Making a 2.0 to 1.9 script would involved consolodating all the various xml files into a single moodle.xml file and using the files.xml information to copy and rename the hash-named files to appropriate directories.  You would, it would seem, loose any 2.0 features In summary, this is not a trivial script and would probably need to be restricted to straight forward courses with no wierd or unknown activities or special configurations.  But it does seem to be possible.  The only other alternative would seem to be to convert an entire site and extract individual courses that might be tested to see how they work in practice, and of course there is no way to go back once the course is underway.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: consolidating courses from two different moodle servers
ResponsesInList.Text: If doing it all in bulk then yes, they may cause a problem, but one at a time, annoying yes, but it will get the job done. The trouble is if you append materials to a course, then you are duplicating a lot of stuff. If you overwrite, delete first then write, you are replacing later materials with older ones. Neither are desirable outcomes, so one course at a time gives you complete control. You may want to append some courses, overwite others but there are about 10 courses you can restore in your 1.9.x without fear of damaging anything, that would be a good place to start.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: consolidating courses from two different moodle servers
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Charlotte, No, you can backup the course with all its files, download to your desktop, and upload to 1.9 server, provided your max upload size is larger than the size of the backup file. You create one course on the 1.9 server and use it to upload each backup file. You then restore each backup to a new course, being careful to give each restoration a unique short name different from any of the 30 on your 1.9 server. This assumes the docs you want are course files and not user files. If, like us, you have a generic teacher in all your classrooms, it may be that some docs belong to a generic user, and then you'll have to backup & restore with user files (&, probably, with users).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: consolidating courses from two different moodle servers
ResponsesInList.Text: Ben is right, there is a couple of issues between 1.8 and 1.9, and most fo those were centred around the plugins - if I remember rightly. So, if I also remember you can backup courses in 1.8 the same way you can in 1.9, that is in sections . What you may be able to do is to backup course files, WITHOUT site files, roles and User files. If this is correct, then do that first. Restore them to 1.9, and you should be able to do so with a minimum of fuss. Quizzes caused the most angst from memory, but there were a number of discussions about those issues in the Quiz forum that you may want to read. Then backup Users and User data, and STUDENT ROLES WITHOUT course files, other roles and site files. Restore them, if you need to. You may be able to restore students without their data, if you want to do it that way, but I cannot remember what functionality is available to you in 1.8... too long ago and not sufficiently well learned to remember much at all before going to 1.9... That is, I suggest, the safest way of doing things, one bit at a time. I know a little time consuming, but safer. If worse comes to worse, you can unzip the files and edit the moodle. xml file to remove anything you do not want in it, rezip them and restore the modified files. There is a lot of xml data in the file that you do not really need to successfully restore courses. If you restore and get a block error, for example, look for the block in the unzipped xml file, delete it and rezip, upload and continue. You may have to remove all references to non-core blocks and some users, Admin user in particular, but it can work.

ResponsesInList.Text: Dear fellow Moodlers, I'm getting a load of error messages when I'm trying to backup my new site. I guess it's a matter of some permission problem somewhere. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: function.mkdir errors
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi. I don't really know much about Moodle, per se, but I do know a lot about PHP and server administration. So, some pointers and questions: The first error, "Warning: mkdir() [function.mkdir]: Permission denied in /var/www/moodle/lib/moodlelib.php on line 6779" is really the only problem. The rest of the errors will almost certainly go away if you can fix this permission problem. The permissions that need to be fixed are on the parent directory of the directory in which a file is being created. (See further description, following these bullets) It is not really a Good Idea(TM) to put your moodledata/ directory in /var/www. It should go directly in /var (i.e. "/var/moodledata") Why? Because putting moodledata/ in /var/www/ makes it directly accessible to anyone with a web browser, unless you are very careful to monitor the permissions and settings of your web server. Okay, so on point 2, here is the explanation. the error said " Permission denied in /var/www/moodle/lib/moodlelib.php" but that is jus tthe line of PHP code that was trying to create a directory. So where is the directory being created? is the question. Well, it looks like (from the subsequent errors) that the problem is in "/var/www/moodledata/temp/backup/1189408008/" The permissions and ownership of /var/www/moodledata/temp/backup/ should be set to allow the "user" who runs the webserver (assuming Apache ) to be able to write to this directory. You will need to know more about the Unix commands: ls -l chmod chown To be able to fix this problem. Please post back later when you get stuck or if you have another question. Seeya...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup of Courses
ResponsesInList.Text: If you want to back up your entire MOODLE, there are three parts that you need to back up (unless you've done something more intelligently than we have).  The three parts are: 1. The Moodle data folder 2. The moodle directory in your wwwroot folder 3. the moodle database . 2 ways that I know of - not sure whiich is technically the correct way. you could have the entire server backed up (all folders/drives etc...). This will mean you have an exct replica which can then be restored if necessary. The second way is to back up the moodle data folder and the wwwroot folder (as you presumably have been doing) and then use whatever database adminstration software you have (Navicat for ourselves, I don't know how to use others) to backup the database (this is where most things other than files are stored). maybe someone will know of a better way, but we use both of these at various times. Graham

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Problema extraño con la copia de seguridad
ResponsesInList.Text: La pantalla de Administración>Cursos>Copia de seguridad es para definir los parámetros para un copia de seguridad programada (no manual). Si dejas en blanco la ubicación de la copia, por omisión ésta se guarda en la carpeta backupdata del curso siendo respaldado. Cuando la copia se hace desde el curso mismo, ésta es manual e inmediata (con la fecha y hora en que se esté creando). La copia siempre se guarda en la carpeta bakcupdata del curso siendo respaldado. El proceso de restauración inicia en la carpeta backup data porque ahí es donde se guardan las copias de seguridad, así que todo está correcto en tu instalación.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moddle2RC1 Restore stops on comfirm page
ResponsesInList.Text: It depends on what operating system you're running - it's different on Unix and Windows machines, but it's usually in your PHP installation folder. So, if you're running Windows and you installed PHP in the C:\PHP folder then the path to it is probably C:\PHP\php.ini. Alternatively it could be in the path specified in the PHPRC environment variable, if that has been set. If not, it could be in the folder specified in the IniFilePath key in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\PHP in your Windows registry. You can also find it using the goold old "Find -> Files or Folders" option on the Start Menu. If you're running a Unix OS then the path is defined at compile time. Most of the time when you compile PHP it puts the ini file in /usr/local/lib/php/. You might be able to type locate php.ini or find / -name php.ini -print and have it tell you the location of the php.ini file. But I'm not a Unix user so...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup advice
ResponsesInList.Text: Apparently when you do automated backups Moodle only backs up the courses that have changed and are available to students , i.e. not hidden. If you don't like this then vote for change: MDL-15256 . The way I get around it is to make a small change to the courses that haven't changed, e.g. I'll enroll a dummy user. It's easy to do that for multiple courses using a flat file .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Failed course backup - timed out?
ResponsesInList.Text: Have you tried backing up a section at a time? Just backup part of the course, then another part and maybe a third part - depending how big it is. Be selective, and make sure you identify exactly what you are backing up in each part. The reason I suggest this is that backing up can take a lot of resources, and if the resources are not available, then is going to spit the dummy at some stage. Should be OK, though. It is possible there is something acting like a furball in an assignment or some such, causing the backup to choke. What should happen is if you have a smaller backup , it should work so you do the next part. If size has been the problem, then it will complete the sectional backup successfully. If it spits in the first part, but not the second, or vice-versa, then try and narrow what you are backing up, until you get a clear backup, then you have a good chance at finding what it is choking on. The alternative is something has gone wrong in your backup pages. To save some time, you might want to FTP a new set of pages for the backup folder. That is, from your Test site, using FTP, delete your backup folder then just replace it with your test site folder. Be much quicker than downloading and updating. Or do this first, try it again, then if it repeats the behaviour, then you have lost nothing - but you have eliminated corruption of the code. Of course, this takes time, and there may be a quicker way of doing this. If you backup parts of the course, then restore it later, just make sure you set the restore to add to the existing course.

As with the zip program, the external program is faster, so if you are experiencing slow backups or other performance problems, try setting the path to your unzip program. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup Moodle Site!?!?!
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi and welcome to the land of Open Doors... I call it that because as a newbie, I went through hell trying to figure out how to do things then realized that I was pushing on doors that were already open.. Firstly, you might want to look at these Moodle Doc pages to get a lot of stuff explained a little more simply, perhaps. Backups are confusing because we are used to just opening a backup program and clicking a few buttons and selecting what we want and forgetting it. Boring... well Moodle is not a lot better... You can automate this process by creating a cron process,(a batch file) from within Moodle using the Administration > Courses > Backup page and schedule regular site backups. Select the options you want and it is really a "set and forget" process and as along as you schedule it for a minimum use period, you should be OK. The cron should just run when scheduled. If you are not sure what options you want, chose different ones, then download the backup file to your test site, and if you do not have one then create one on a standalone computer or laptop these are essential, and restore to see what you get. Refine your selections as you gain experience. Of course, you can use external software to select what you want to backup and how often you want to backup and it will be just as valid. I think Bluehost will have something to help you there... If this is all you have had to keep you awake at night then you have done very well so far, for not being a web guy!!! Cheers...

This may or may not be useful to others, depending on how their courses and school calendars are set up. Best, Buddy

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup still not working
ResponsesInList.Text: It might possibly be your SELinux settings preventing write access by Apache (httpd) on your data directory if you have SELinux set for Enforcing. Enforcing is turned on by default on your typical Linux install nowdays. Because of the way I update my Linux server I have to make sure to reset mine each time I do an upgrade to Moodle. If you have admin shell access to the site you can check easily by temporarily switching to permissive mode. If the backup then works you know that is the problem.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup still not working

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup still not working
ResponsesInList.Text: If you have admin shell access to the site you can check easily by temporarily switching to permissive mode. If the backup then works you know that is the problem. # setenforce 0 Try your backup then switch back to enforcing. # setenforce 1 On my system the security messages tell me what to type in to fix it, which is usually: # chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t '/var/www/moodle/data' James, As I mentioned above, enforcement is something I only know how to do when in via shell/terminal mode on my server. It can also be done from a terminal while logged in directly on the server. Another way to do it, which is mostly what I use, is that I run a program call WinSCP (free program) on my desktop windows computer. It lets me log in remotely to my server with two ftp style windows-the left one is local files and the right one is the files on my Linux server. Lets me drag and drop files to and from my server, which makes it very easy to do upgrades and file/folder transfers to Moodle. Two of the commands available from the Command menu in WinSCP is to open a Terminal window or open a terminal window via Putty. I prefer Putty (you have to also install Putty) but in either case you can then use the getenforce and setenforce Linux commands for SELinux. Hope this makes it a little clearer. AL

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Backup still not working
ResponsesInList.Text: James, It's not in the httpd folder To disable immediately (command line) run: setenforce 0 To disable after reboot edit the file /etc/selinux/conf: SELINUX=disabled Save it and reboot. You can also append the following to your kernel line in grub selinux=0

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Saving a course for re-use
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Rory You have a couple of options here, one is to backup the course which creates a zip file that can be restored into another course or into a new course. If you go this way you can select to import only the quiz if you like or all activities. Another option is to export the quiz questions from this course and import them into another course. If you go this way I suggest exporting as Moodle XML format, you'll also have to re-create the quiz activity as this only deals with the questions.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Saving a course for re-use

What I have developed for my self is a hidden backup course where I keep a copy of all my quizzes/glossaries/assignments/etc. If you do not have admin/course creation privileges, have the admin make it for you and set it so that only you and a fake student (for testing) account have access. Then, I use the Sharing Cart to move a copy of them to wherever I need it. So far I've only found one thing I could not move this way...Real Time Quizzes...but there might be others. The nice thing about using this method, is that I always have a copy of whatever assignment/quiz/ lesson etc. online that I can take/tryout/modify without it impacting my active class the students are using. Hope this helps.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Migrate a course from Blackboard to Moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: That's a lot of questions! I'll try to answer as many as I can. The way you did it (creating a new empty course, then restoring "into" it) should work, but I agree that it is counterintuitive. If you have course creator privileges (e.g., if you are an admin), then you do not need an empty course. Say you were admin. On the front page of your site, click Administration -> Front page -> Front page restore, browse to your zip file, upload it, and click Restore. You will be given the option (later in the process) to either (1) add content to an existing course or (2) create a new course. I believe that Moodle will automatically recognize a Blackboard file. I believe the migration tool is no longer necessary. If your Bb file is greater than your upload limit, you must increase your upload limit. See http://docs.moodle.org/en/Administration_FAQ

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Migrate a course from Blackboard to Moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Jeffrey! I have done a lot of these conversions. I always create a "conversions and uploads" course where I upload all moodle or BB files prior to restoring them. In this case, you will find restore in the "restore" area in your admin menu. If you do not have this block in the uploads and conversions course (or whatever course you are using), perhaps you just need to activate it (as Miguel says, above). It shows up as a link among all the other tools. You will need the xslt library installed, I think. Do you have that? Otherwise, the BB restore should be "built in" to moodle as of moodle 1.5. The reason for this is that I had a corrupted archive once and it blew up when I restored it. My moodle was rather damaged as a result, and I didn't take that chance again. I do think that this was because my BB database was ailing dreadfully at the time, but it was rather shocking. You may find some vagaries with your quiz pools. BB5.5 archived them differently than later versions of BB, so you might want to check your restored course to see if all of it came over. I did have to export the quiz items separately because we were using the older version. Last, if you can't upload a file more than 2 MB, if you have server access you can FTP the file (or use the windows explorer) to place it in the uploads and conversions course area directly. It will be some folder corresponding to the course ID number in the moodle data directory. That is a way around the limit if you can't change that on your server. So those are my stories!
